thread.title: China's iPhone Sales Ban Isn't a Big Deal For Apple

title: China's iPhone Sales Ban Isn't a Big Deal For Apple
text:
China’s iPhone Sales Ban Isn’t a Big Deal For Apple By Dec. 10, 2018 11:17 a.m. ET Order Reprints iPhone 7 Photograph by Sara Kurfeß Text size
Apple stock continued its selloff Monday after Qualcomm appeared to score a minor win in its yearslong patent conflict with the iPhone-maker, but the reality may be only a symbolic victory.
A Chinese intellectual-property court found Apple (ticker: AAPL) in violation of two of Qualcomm’s (QCOM) patents and banned the sale of models from 2015’s iPhone 6S through 2017’s iPhone X in the country. Apple stock was down more than 2% Monday morning, while Qualcomm rose 3.3%.
“We have an abiding belief in the need to protect intellectual property rights,” Qualcomm general counsel Don Rosenberg said in a statement. “Apple continues to benefit from our intellectual property while refusing to compensate us.”
Both of the patents in question relate to software and are separate from hardware patents under dispute in other court battles between the two tech giants in the U.S. and elsewhere. According to Apple, iOS 12, the newest version of the iPhone operating system, doesn’t violate the two patents. Any new iPhones sold would presumably be running the latest software and not be subject to the ban.
Apple isn’t required to pay any damages or fines.
Apple questioned Qualcomm’s motives. “Qualcomm’s effort to ban our products is another desperate move by a company whose illegal practices are under investigation by regulators around the world,” Apple said in a statement Monday morning. “All iPhone models remain available for our customers in China.”
The company said it plans to pursue all its legal options. Newsletter Sign-up
The injunction doesn’t appear likely to materially affect iPhone sales in China. Apple’s latest iPhone models, including the XS, XS Max, and XR, weren’t included. “While the headlines are concerning regarding this latest China court ruling, we believe the models involved are related to 10%-15% of sales” in the region, wrote Wedbush analyst Daniel Ives in a report Monday morning.
A quick visit to Apple’s Chinese website on Monday showed XS, XS Max, and XR, plus the iPhone 7, 7 Plus, 8, and 8 Plus—phones that nominally would have been affected by the ban—still available for sale.
The court ruling may add to Apple’s desire to stop doing business with Qualcomm. The company has already begun using Intel (INTC) chips in its iPhones, but remains in multiple disputes around the world over the use of technologies covered by Qualcomm’s extensive patent portfolio.
